explain.say: A tree branch falls across a line, a digger hits a cable, lightning flashes over an insulator. In an instant the current takes a short cut and surges far above normal. On the board, an 11 kilovolt bus is fed by a 20 megavolt-ampere transformer, drawn for one phase. It is carrying its rated load, about 1.05 kiloamps. The fault path is still open.

explain.say: Look at the transformer's reactance, the only thing between the source and a fault. Its nameplate says 5 percent impedance, 0.05 per unit. The base impedance is 11 squared over 20, 6.05 ohms, so the transformer is just 0.30 ohms, tiny next to the 6.05 ohm load. What happens when something bypasses the load?

explain.say: Close the fault path. Now only 0.30 ohms is left, so the current jumps to 6351 volts over 0.3025 ohms, about 21 kiloamps, twenty times normal. Watch the dots race. In per unit it is even quicker: fault current is 1 over 0.05, which is 20 per unit. So does a smaller transformer impedance make faults better or worse?

faq.q: How do you calculate fault current?
faq.a: For a three-phase fault at a transformer's terminals, fault current is rated current divided by the per-unit impedance. A 20 megavolt-ampere, 11 kilovolt transformer has a rated current of about 1.05 kiloamps, so with 5 percent impedance the fault current is about 21 kiloamps.
asks: What is the fault current formula?

faq.q: What is fault level in MVA?
faq.a: Fault level is the three-phase fault power at a point: root 3 times the rated voltage times the fault current, or simply the base megavolt-amperes divided by the per-unit impedance. 20 over 0.05 gives 400 megavolt-amperes.

faq.q: What is the most common type of fault?
faq.a: Single line to ground faults, where one conductor touches earth or a grounded object, make up about 70 to 80 percent of faults on overhead lines. Three-phase faults are the rarest.

faq.q: Why does transformer impedance limit fault current?
faq.a: During a short circuit the load is bypassed, so only the source and transformer impedance remain. A transformer with lower percent impedance lets more fault current flow, so impedance is chosen with fault levels in mind.

faq.q: What happens if a breaker cannot handle the fault current?
faq.a: If the fault current exceeds the breaker's breaking capacity, it may fail to interrupt the arc and can be destroyed, spreading the damage. That is why breaker ratings are chosen from fault-level studies.

facts: A transformer with 5% impedance gives a terminal fault current of about 20 times its rated current.
Single line-to-ground faults make up roughly 70–80% of faults on overhead lines.
Fault level in MVA equals the base MVA divided by the per-unit impedance to the fault.
